consensus_summary: The mainstream consensus reads 'gnashing of teeth' (usually in the fixed Synoptic formula 'weeping and gnashing of teeth') as stock imagery for the extreme anguish, despair, and remorse of those condemned and excluded at eschatological judgment, traditionally located in hell/conscious punishment. A well-recognized secondary reading (listed as 'common' by most responses) takes the gnashing as hostile rage against God or the righteous, citing Ps 35:16, Ps 37:12, Ps 112:10, Acts 7:54; annihilationist and covenantal/AD-70 readings are noted as minority positions.
book_summary: The book identifies gnashing of teeth as the rage of the wicked directed at the righteous — sorrow and hatred combined in the excluded as they behold the kingdom they forfeited — followed by their dissolution ('then they melt away'). It anchors the symbol in Ps 37:12 (the wicked gnashing at the just), Acts 7:54 (Stephen's trial), and the Ps 112:10 template (see, be grieved, gnash, perish), and explicitly distinguishes itself from the common teaching of conscious everlasting torment.
consensus_core_identification: Anguish/despairing remorse of the condemned under eschatological judgment and exclusion, conventionally understood within conscious punishment in hell.
book_core_identification: Rage-and-grief of the wicked aimed at the righteous upon seeing the kingdom they lost, terminating in their perishing ('melt away'), not ongoing torment.
boundary_disagreement: The book reclassifies the emotional register from despairing remorse under torment to hostile rage directed at the righteous, and it reclassifies the outcome from everlasting conscious suffering to terminal destruction (Ps 112:10 'melt away... perish'). It also broadens the symbol's extension to include this-life gnashing at the just (Ps 37:12, Acts 7:54) as definitional instances of the same symbol, whereas the consensus treats the Synoptic eschatological formula as primary and the OT/Acts usage as background.
material_contradiction: The book's denial of conscious everlasting torment contradicts the traditional doctrinal setting the consensus attaches to the phrase, but this concerns surrounding eschatology rather than replacing the symbol's referent; the consensus itself flags both the rage reading (common) and the annihilationist reading (minority) as recognized alternatives, so the identification is not a replacement of the central referent.
rationale: The book keeps the consensus's general referent — the reaction of the wicked/excluded confronted with divine judgment and the kingdom they lost — but materially shifts its characterization and boundaries: rage at the righteous rather than remorseful anguish, and a terminal ('melt away') rather than everlasting condition. Both elements appear in the blind responses as listed alternatives (rage: 'common' in A, B, D; annihilationism: 'minority' in A, B), so the book elevates and combines recognized alternatives against the primary reading. This is real boundary disagreement without replacement of the central referent, fitting REFINED rather than DIVERGENT or NOVEL.
strongest_objection: One could argue DIVERGENT: the book's common-view note explicitly rejects the mainstream framing (anguish under conscious everlasting torment), and 'rage at the righteous ending in perishing' arguably replaces 'remorseful anguish of the damned in ongoing torment' as an incompatible identification of what the gnashing is. However, since the consensus responses themselves list both the rage reading and the annihilationist reading as recognized alternatives, and the central referent (the excluded's reaction at judgment) is preserved, REFINED remains the better fit.
